source_text: Reddamus nunc rationem quare hominem ipsum fecerit: quod si philosophi scissent, aut defendissent illa quae uera inuenerant aut in maximos errores non incidissent. haec enim summa, hic cardo rerum est, quem qui non tenuerit, ueritas illi omnis elabitur, hoc est denique, quod efficiat illis non quadrare rationem: quae illis si adfulsisset, si sacramentum hominis omne cognossent, numquam disputationes eorum et omnem philosophiam de transuerso Academia iugulasset. sicut ergo mundum non propter se deus fecit, quia commodis eius non indiget, sed propter hominem, qui eo utitur, ita ipsum hominem propter se. quae utilitas deo in homine, inquit Epicurus ut eum propter se faceret? scilicet ut esset qui opera eius intellegeret, qui prouidentiam disponendi, rationem faciendi, uirtutem consummandi et sensu admirari et uoce proloqui posset: quorum omnium summa haec est, ut deum colat. is enim colit qui haec intellegit, is artificem rerum omnium, is uerum patrem suum debita ueneratione prosequitur qui uirtutem maiestatis eius de suorum operum inuentione inceptione « perfectione metitur. quod planius argumentum proferri potest et mundum hominis et hominem sua causa deum fecisse, quam quod ex omnibus animantibus solus ita formatus est, ut oculi eius ad caelum directi, facies ad deum spectans, uultus cum suo parente communis sit uideaturque hominem deus quasi porrecta manu adleuatum ex humo ad contemplationem sui excitasse? quid ergo inquit deo cultus hominis confert beato et nulla re indigenti? uel si tantum honoris homini habuit, ut ipsius causa mundum fabricaret, ut instrueret eum sapientia, ut dominum uiuentium faceret eumque diligeret tamquam filium, cur mortalem fragilemque constituit? cur omnibus malis quem diligebat obiecit, cum oporteret et beatum esse hominem tamquam coniunctum ac proximum deo et perpetuum, sicut est ipse, ad quem colendum et contemplandum figuratus est? quamquam haec fere in prioribus libris sparsim docuimus, tamen quoniam: proprie id materia nunc exigit, qua de uita beata disserere propositum est, explicanda sunt ista diligentius et plenius, ut dispositio dei et opus uoluntasque noscatur.
pass_a_gloss: We will now give the reason why God created man himself: which if the philosophers had known, they would have either defended those things which they had truly discovered or they would not have fallen into the greatest errors. For this is the sum, this is the hinge of things, which whoever has not held, all truth will slip away from him, that is, finally, what makes their reason not fit together: which if it had shone upon them, if they had known the whole mystery of man, they would never have cut down their own disputes and all philosophy with the sword of the Academy from side to side. Just as, therefore, God did not create the world for its own sake, because He does not need its benefits, but for the sake of man, who uses it, so He created man for His own sake. What usefulness, says Epicurus, is there to God in man, that He should create him for His own sake? Namely, that there should be someone who could understand His works, who could arrange providence, reason out actions, complete virtue, and admire with his senses and proclaim with his voice: the sum of all these things is that he may worship God. For he worships who understands these things, he who with due veneration follows the true Father of all things, the Artificer, who measures the virtue of His majesty from the invention, beginning, and perfection of His works. What plainer argument can be brought forward, that God created both the world and man for His own sake, than that among all living things man alone is so formed that his eyes are directed towards heaven, his face looks towards God, his countenance seems to be in common with his Parent, and it appears that God has raised man up from the earth to the contemplation of Himself as if with outstretched hand? What, therefore, does the worship of man confer upon God, who is blessed and in need of nothing? Or if God had so much honor for man that He created the world for his sake, that He might instruct him with wisdom, that He might make him the lord of living things, and that He might love him like a son, why did He establish him as mortal and fragile? Why did He expose him to all evils, whom He loved, when it was fitting that man should be blessed, like one connected to and near to God, and perpetual, just as God Himself is, for whom he was formed to worship and contemplate? Although we have taught these things scattered throughout the previous books, nevertheless, since the subject matter now properly demands it, with which we have proposed to discuss the blessed life, these things must be explained more diligently and fully, so that the disposition of God and His work and will may be known.
pass_b_english: We must now explain why God created humanity. Had the philosophers grasped this, they would have defended the truths they did discover, or at least avoided the gravest errors. This point is the sum and hinge of everything; without it, all truth slips away, and reason itself fails to cohere. If this light had dawned on them—if they had known the full mystery of man—their disputes and the whole of philosophy would never have been cut down by the sword of Academic skepticism.

Just as God did not make the world for its own sake—He has no need of its benefits—but for the sake of man who uses it, so He made man for His own sake. Epicurus asks what usefulness man could have for God, that He should create him for Himself. The answer: so there would be someone able to understand God's works, to arrange providence, to reason out actions, to perfect virtue, to admire with the senses and proclaim with the voice. The sum of all these capacities is that man may worship God. For the one who understands these things worships; the one who, with due reverence, follows the true Father and Artificer of all, measuring the virtue of His majesty by the invention, beginning, and perfection of His works.

What plainer argument could show that God made both the world and man for His own sake than this: among all living creatures, man alone is formed with eyes directed toward heaven, a face looking toward God, a countenance that seems to share a likeness with his Parent? It appears that God has lifted man from the earth to the contemplation of Himself, as with an outstretched hand. What, then, does man's worship add to a blessed God who lacks nothing? Or if God honored man so highly that He created the world for him, instructed him with wisdom, made him lord of living things, and loved him like a son, why did He make him mortal and fragile? Why did He expose the one He loved to every evil, when it would have been fitting for man to be blessed—joined to and near God, perpetual as God Himself is—for whose worship and contemplation he was formed?

Although we have touched on these points scattered through the earlier books, the present subject—the discussion of the blessed life—properly demands them. Therefore they must be explained more diligently and fully, so that God's disposition, work, and will may be known.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal clause-by-clause translation, while Pass B provides a fluent rendering. Both preserve the nuances of the Latin, including the Epicurean interjection and the rhetorical questions regarding man's mortality and fragility. The title 'Why God Created Man' correctly identifies the thought of the passage.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the meaning, structure, and key theological arguments. The citations and terminology are consistent with the source. No errors or omissions are detected in the translation.
